First, we get the RS data set and clean it up.

Note, that this default RS data set in the rENA package is a MESS. There are duplicated lines, and there are no mentors included in the data. We should probably do something about that.

```{r get_data}

d = RS.data

#function to get rid of factors
factor.to.value = function(x) {
  y = as.character(x)
  z = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(y))
  if(any(is.na(z))) return(y)
  return (z)
}

#clean up factors in data
d = mutate_if(d, is.factor, factor.to.value)

```

Next, we define some helper functions that make some tasks easier.

```{r HelperFunctions}

#function to convert timestamps
convert.time = function(time.column,
                        format = "%m/%d/%Y %H:%M", 
                        precision = 4, 
                        zero = TRUE, 
                        units = "minutes"
                        ){

    #fix number of significant digits
    options(digits.secs = precision)
    #convert to POSIX time (time in seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00.00 UTC)
    #see function documentation for details
    posix.time = as.POSIXct(time.column, format=format )
    
    #in most cases we just want a number, as POSIX does funny things to dates
    times = as.numeric(posix.time)
    #if requested, set earliest date in set to 0
    if (zero) times = times - min(times)

    #convert to time scale
    #if units are none of these, the return DAYS
    if(units != "seconds") {times = times / 60
    } else {if(units != "minutes") {times = times / 60
    } else {if(units != "hours") {times = times /24}
    }}
    
    return( times )
}


#function allows a call to a functionA inside functionB where functionA can be a...
#   ...fucntion call
#   ...an equation written out
#   ...a character string for a function

call_eq <- function(x = 1, eq = "x^3 + 2*x^2 + x - 7") {
  eq_sub <- substitute(eq)
  if(is.function(eq)) {
    eq(x)
  }
  else if(is.call(eq_sub)) {
    eval(substitute(eq))
  }
  else {
    if(is.name(eq_sub)) {
      eval(substitute(eval(eq_sub)))
    }
    eval(parse(text = eq))
  }
}

#function to merge and reordeer based on column of row numbers that needs to be specified
#uses a bit of tidyverse trickery
#adds 
merge.on = function(x, y, order.column = NA) {
  if(any(names(x) != names(y))) stop("Objects x and y must have the same column names")
  #get rows that are only in x
  unique.x = anti_join(x,y, by = names(x))
  #add rows only inb x to all of y (since y+x will now have all of x and all of y without repeats)
  output = rbind(unique.x,y)
  #if row number column is not specified, try to use the first column
  if (is.na(order.column)) order.column = names(x)[1]
  if (length(order.column) > 1) stop(
    "Can only sort on one column (order.column must be a single column name or number)")
  #order and return
  output = output[order(output[,order.column]), ]
  return(output)
}


#function takes a data frame and returns the value for each column if it has one
##or, if there is more than one value in a column, returns NA for that column
get.unique.col.values = function(df){
  output = data.frame(matrix(NA, nrow = 1, ncol = ncol(df)))
  names(output) = names(df)
  for (this.col in names(df)) {
      this.value = unique(df[,this.col])
      if(length(this.value) == 1) output[1,this.col] = this.value
  } 
  return(output)
}

#used to make test data frames
#creates df by rows rather than columns (which I find more intutive)
test.df = function(data, rows = NA, columns = NA){
  if(is.na(rows)) if(is.na(columns)) {stop("Need rows or columns")
    } else {rows = length(data)/columns}
  if(is.na(columns)) columns = length(data)/rows
  return(data.frame(t(matrix(data, nrow = columns, ncol = rows))))
}

#used to get column names from a data frame in a way that makes them easy to 
#put into a function call 
get.quoted.columns = function(x, as.one.line = FALSE){
  n = names(x)
#  for (i in n) cat('"', i,'"', ifelse(as.one.line, "' ", ",\n"))
  for (i in n) cat("'", i, "'", ifelse(as.one.line, ", ", ",\n"), sep = "")
  return(NULL)
}
```

Next, we need to convert the timestamps in the RSdata set into useable numbers.

Note that we also need to get an estimate of the time gap between utterances in order to convert from data about referents to times.

We have data on referents from Michael Tschol

His data showed:

Furthest referent	Percent
0	                1
1	                0.975961538
2	                0.65625
3	                0.355769231
4	                0.180288462
5	                0.048076923
6	                0.019230769
7	                0.014423077
8	                0.004807692
9	                0

These is a survivorship analysis. So 18% of lines had their furthest referent 4 lines OR FEWER back in the data.

We thus use a WEIGHTING of .18 for an utterance that is 4 turns back. Why? Because ON AVERAGE, that is the expected value of the contribution from an utternace that far back.

But here we need times, so we find the average time between utterances -- leaving out the gaps between days.

The analysis below (see histogram) showed that there were a lot of outliers in the time lags: the mean was 2.8 minutes, which by inspeection of the data seemed like a long time. 

The mean lag for chats less than 10 minutes apart was .78, which seemed like a more reasonable estimate, given the data.

Tschol suggested a window size of 4 or 5, with the idea that there were few additional chats that were going to be included after that, and we would likely be including things in the recent temporal context that were not actually referents.

This would make the average RCT something on the order of 3-4 minutes, which, again, seems reasonable.

This meant that we needed a decay function that modeled this curve:

Minutes	Decay
0	      1
0.78	  0.975961538
1.56	  0.65625
2.34	  0.355769231
3.12	  0.180288462
3.9	    0.048076923
4.68	  0.019230769
5.46	  0.014423077
6.24	  0.004807692

I cheated a bit for now and put the data in Excel, and used a polynomial trendline, coming up with 

y = -0.0059x4 + 0.0806x3 - 0.3186x2 + 0.1178x + 1
R² = 0.9948

We'll have to develop some r function to do this kind of estimation at some point. The current version is wildly overfit, but in this case that isn't really so bad, as we are really just INTERPOLATING rather than EXTRAPOLATING from this function.

Note that I am not using an exponential decay function because it doesn't fit the data as well. The data looks something like this:

|
|
•  •  
|     •
|         •
|               •
|______________________•__________•

The little plateau makes it hard to fit with an exponential. Not saying we shouldn't do that anyway, but for this experiment it didn't seem like the right choice.


```{r determineDecayFunction}



#from tscholl
#modeled in Excel for now... will need to write a function to generate this equation from raw data

#y = -0.0059x4 + 0.0806x3 - 0.3186x2 + 0.1178x + 1
#R² = 0.9948


#specific function for these decay values
decay.function = function(x) return(-0.0059*x^4 + 0.0806*x^3 - 0.3186*x^2 + 0.1178*x + 1)

```

Next, I developed functions to compute the decay for giveen a time for a current event (now) and a time or times for events in the past (event.time).

The function get.decay works with just a single decay function. 

As the example shows, get.decay.modes works if you specify a named LIST of funcitons that correspond to some data column with information about the modalities in the data (eg, page view v chat).

Thanks to Cody for the call_eq function that this uses. That was a pin to figure out for me.


```{r}

#define generic function to retuen decay calues 
#TIME IS IN MINUTES
get.decay = function(now, event.time=0, decay.function) {
  #trap for POSIX times
  times = as.numeric(event.time)
  
  #compute lag
  x = as.numeric(now) - times
  #trap negative lag times (ie, events in the future)
  ok.values = (x>=0)

  #initialize output
  output = rep(0, length(x))
  if(any(ok.values)) {
    #compute decay
    decays = call_eq(x = x[ok.values], eq = decay.function(x))
    #zero out negative decays
    decays[decays<0] = 0
    output[ok.values] = decays
    }
  return(output)
} 




get.decay.modes = function(
  now,
  event.time=0,
  modes = NA,
  decay.function
) {
  
  #if modes not specifieed, assume a single decay function and call get.decay
  if (any(is.na(modes))) {
    return(get.decay(now, event.time, decay.function))
  }
   
  #again, trap POSIX if that is how times are given
  times = as.numeric(event.time)

  #compute lag
  x = as.numeric(now) - times
  
  #initialize output
  decays = rep(0, length(x))
  
  #abort if negative values are given
  if(any(x<0)) stop("negative values not permitted in decay times [get.decay.modes]")
  
  #get decays based on function given in list with name from modes
  #heart of the call here is the decay.function[[modes[i]]]
  #this pulls the function from the list decay.function[[  ]] with the same name modes[i] 
  #as the mode of the current event i
  for (i in 1:length(x)) decays[i] = call_eq(x = x[i], eq = decay.function[[modes[i]]])
  
  #zero out negative results
  #necessary because polynomial decay functions can go negative outside of scope
  #(They can also get wildly positive, but I couldn't think how to trap that)
  decays[decays<0] = 0
  return(decays)
}

#TEST code 
my.modes = c("m2", "m3", "m2", "m2")
my.test.decay = list()
my.test.decay$m2 = function(x) return(2*x)
my.test.decay$m3 = function(x) return(3*x)

get.decay.modes(now = 5, event.time = 1:4, modes = my.modes, decay.function = my.test.decay)

get.decay.modes(now = 3, event.time = 1:2, decay.function = decay.function)

rm(my.modes)
rm(my.test.decay)
 
```

OK, so now we need to find the CONTEXTS for each unit of analysis in the data. The context is basically the horizon of observation (HOO) for each unit -- the things (chats, documents, galvanic skin response) that they are aware of and thus can "respond" to. (We are using "aware of" in a general sense here. We are not *directly* aware of our galvanic skin response, but we do respond to the stress it reflects.)


```{r functionToGetHOOcontexts}

#function to get contexts for each unit, by hoo.rules
#returns a list of dataframes (one for each context) in $contexts
#plus metadata that ena will need
get.contexts = function(units, data, hoo.rules){
    
    #This is a hack I use to create functions. When I start, I assign these
    #temporary names to variables. I can assign values and step through the function
    #while I am writing/deebugging. Then when the function works, I can create the function
    #call and pass the parameters to these termporary variables.
    f.data = data
    f.units = units
    f.hoo = hoo.rules

    #add row numbeers to the data (needed to keep data sorted)
    Rows = 1:nrow(f.data)
    f.data.augmented = cbind(Rows, f.data)
    
    #initialize output list for contexts
    hoos = list()
    
    #loop over units
    for(i in 1:nrow(f.units)){
      this.unit = f.units[i,]
    
      #initialize this hoo
      hoos[[i]] = list()
      hoos[[i]][["context"]] = f.data.augmented[0,] #quick hack to create a blank copy of an
                                                    #existing matrix
      
      #get this unit data -- semi join takes thing from the left variable that match
      #things from the right variable in the columns in BY
      this.unit.data = semi_join(f.data.augmented, this.unit, by = names(this.unit))
      
      #assign meta data for unit
      #create a list of named list with names equal to unit columns
      for(j in names(this.unit)) hoos[[i]][["unit"]][j] = this.unit[,j]
      #put in values for this unit
      hoos[[i]][["unit"]] = 
        as.data.frame(
          t(hoos[[i]][["unit"]]), 
          col.names = names(hoos[[i]][["unit"]])
          )
 
      # for this unit, process each context rule 
      for(this.rule in f.hoo){
        
        #initialize context with all data
        #we will remove things that don't fit
        this.output = f.data.augmented
        
        #loop over conditions in each rule to extract data
        for(k in 1:length(this.rule)){
          
          this.condition = this.rule[[k]]
          #get the column name this condition applies to
          this.col = names(this.rule[k])
          
          #replace <UNIT> with data from this unit and filter by those values
          if(this.condition == "<UNIT>") {
                #get values for column for this unit
                this.values = as.data.frame(unique(this.unit.data[,this.col]))
                names(this.values) = this.col
                #select rows with these values in the column
                this.output = semi_join(this.output, this.values, by = this.col)
          }
          
          #or, select rows that match the given regex
          else{
          this.output = subset(this.output, 
                               grepl(this.condition,
                                     this.output[,this.col]
                                     )
                                )
          }

    
        }#finished with all conditions for this rule
      
        #if this is the first rulw (or otherwise the list is empty), store temporary output
        if (nrow(hoos[[i]][["context"]]) == 0) hoos[[i]][["context"]] = this.output
    
        #otherwise, merge new temporary output into existing
        #This merge function removes duplicate rows and keeps output in the order
        #of column "Rows"
        else hoos[[i]][["context"]] = merge.on(hoos[[i]][["context"]], this.output, "Rows")
    
              
      }#finished with rules
    
      #remove row numbers
      hoos[[i]][["context"]] = hoos[[i]][["context"]][,-1]
    
    }#finished with unit  
  
  #add unit names to context lists
  output.names = c()
  for (this.hoo in 1:length(hoos)) {
    output.names = c(output.names, paste(hoos[[this.hoo]]$unit, collapse = "::"))
  }
  names(hoos) = output.names
  
  #begin constructing output

  output = list()             #initialize output list
  output$contexts = hoos      #store named contexts
  output$hoo.rules = f.hoo    #add rules used
  
  #add information ENA needs
  output$units = f.units      #units  
  output$raw.data = f.data    #raw data

return(output)

}#end of function


```


Here we test the function on an attenuated data set (easier to check outputs). You can remove the limit on the size of the data set in the first line below.

For the test, we assign a set of fake "modes" to the data (in this casee, chat and page view). 

The get context function also requires that you supply the data columns for users. This is so that it is possible to get contexts for only some of the users.

We assign HOO rules to a list of lists.

The first level has an (unnamed) list for each rule.

The next level has a NAMED list where each name is the column the condition should apply to, and the content of the list is a string where options are...
   ...<UNIT>, which is replaced by the value of the individual unit 
               for which context is being constructed
   ...any regex
   
The funciton will include rows of data that match ALL of the conditions of ANY rule.

The test here shows two cases:

1. Subset by condition and group, as in regular ENA
2. Subset by condition and group, but with ALL data modes for the unit and only chats for confederates

```{r maskHelperFunction}

mask = function(df,                         #data frame to apply mask on
                mask,                       #mask (vector with ncol same as df, or matrix with 
                                            #same size as original)
                convertMaskToVector = T,    #if true, mask is in the for of an adjacency matrix,
                                            #which gets converted to a vector
                undirectedModel = T,        #setting for directed or undirected model (only used
                                            #if convertMaskToVector = TRUE)
                dfIsMatrixOfVectors = T){   #when true, df is a set of adjacency vectors;
                                            #when false, df is 
  
  if (dfIsMatrixOfVectors) {
    
    if (convertMaskToVector) {
      if(undirectedModel) {
        mask = mask[upper.tri(mask)]
      } else {
          mask = as.vector(mask)
        }
    } 
    print(mask)
    for (i in 1:nrow(df)){
      df[i,] = df[i,] * mask
    }
    
    output = df
    
  } else {
    
    output = df * mask
    
  }
  
  return(output)
  
}

```

So, now we're ready to make a decay model.

The basic approach of the model is to loop over the contexts from the get.contexts function. Each context is associated with one unit of analysis, and carries all of the rows of data that the unit can "see".

So, we do some initializing of variables, and then loop over the contexts. 

We start by pulkling out all of the rows that have no codes in them -- they don't contribute anything to the analysis, and we don't need them as "spacer" rows to track windows. 

In each context, we pull out the "receiving" rows -- that is, the rows that belong to the unit -- and loop over those. If there aren't any (after pulling out the zero rows) then we skip the unit.

For each response row, we find the rows in the context that happen before the response. These are the ground. (We can also specify a maximum time back in time if the data file is very large and we want to save a little processing time.)

We then apply the decay function to the ground codes -- or if it is a multi-model model, then we apply thee decay functions based on the modes specified. The do that, pass the current time, the time of each row in the ground, and the mode of each row in the ground to a function that computes the decays. We use matrix multiplication to apply the vector of decays to the ground codes.

Once the decays are added, we process the data much like ENA: there is a window (the ground) and a response, we do matrix multiplication and then subtract the response-to-response diagonal so we are not counting self-references within the response line.

A weighting function is then applied (default is sqrt), to account for the same weighting issues that come up in a weighted ENA model of over-weighting rows with high code-counts.

TMA does this as a directed matrix, and then at the very end, the undirected matrix is computed from the directed. Both are returned.

Finally, the function converts the adjacency matrices (directed and undirected) into a table of adjacency vectors.

Information needed to make an ENA set with the undirected adjacency vectors is passed to ena.set to construct a properly-formatted ENA set. *Note that this does not work at the moment, but Cody is going to look into it.*

All of the above functionality should work. That is, models can be run as uni- or multi-modal, with or without time limits on the lookback, with or without meta data.

```{r makeDecayModel}

#default decay function, falls from 1-0 over time 4
#this is used if someone does not specify a decay function, or doesn't know 
#how to calculate one

#we could get more creative and let someone specify how long they want the
#decay to go and then give them a function based on that
default.decay.function = function(x) ifelse(
  x<4,
  return(max(0, (0.0508*x^3 - 0.3035*x^2 + 0.1532*x + 1))),
  return(0)
)


accumulate.units = function(context.object, 
                            time.column = NA,  #if no time column is given, 
                                               #use model with equal time = 1 between lines in a hoo
                            codes, 
                            decay.function = default.decay.function, 
                            mode.column = NA, 
                            mask = NA,
                            time.limit = NA,
                            weight.by = sqrt,
                            meta.data = NA,
                            return.ena.set = TRUE
                            ){
f.window.limit = time.limit
f.contexts = context.object$contexts
f.codes = codes
f.time = time.column
f.decay = decay.function
f.mode = mode.column
f.weighting.function = weight.by
f.meta.data = meta.data
f.units = context.object$units
f.raw = context.object$raw.data

use.modes = ifelse(any(is.na(f.mode)), FALSE, TRUE)
use.meta = ifelse(any(is.na(f.meta.data)), FALSE, TRUE)
use.mask = ifelse(is.matrix(mask), TRUE, FALSE)
use.window = ifelse(any(is.na(f.time)), TRUE, FALSE)

#create undirected mask if there are NAs in lower triangle of given mask
if (any(is.na(mask[lower.tri(mask)]))) {mask[lower.tri(mask)] = mask[upper.tri(mask)]}

#initialize metadata matrix, if needed
if(use.meta) {
  output.meta.data = f.raw[0,c(names(f.units),f.meta.data) %>% unique]
}

#initialize adjacency vector matrices
undirected.adjacency.vectors = as.matrix(
  data.frame(matrix(NA, nrow = 1, ncol = ncol(rENA:::namesToAdjacencyKey(f.codes))))[0,]
)
directed.adjacency.vectors = as.matrix(
  data.frame(matrix(NA, nrow = 1, ncol = length(f.codes)^2)[0,])
)


#create blank code matrix template
n = length(f.codes)
blank.code.matrix = matrix(0, n, n)
colnames(blank.code.matrix) = f.codes
rownames(blank.code.matrix) = f.codes
#blank.code.matrix

#loop over contexts
for (this.hoo in 1:length(f.contexts)) {
  #initialize connection  matrix for this unit
  this.code.matrix = blank.code.matrix
  
  #get data from this context
  this.context = f.contexts[[this.hoo]]$context
  

  #if using a time model
  #remove rows with no codes from the data
  #we don't need them as "spacers" for the rest of the data
  #because we are using time to define our connections
  if (!use.window) {
    this.context = this.context[rowSums(as.matrix(this.context[,f.codes])) > 0,]
  }
  #set row numbers
  Rows = 1:nrow(this.context)
  f.data.augmented = cbind(Rows, this.context)

  #get unit name
  this.unit = f.contexts[[this.hoo]]$unit
  
  #find rows belonging to unit
  this.unit.data = semi_join(f.data.augmented, this.unit, by = names(this.unit))
  
  #get meta data for this unit and add to the the meta data dataframe
   if(use.meta) {
      # browser();
      output.meta.data = rbind(output.meta.data, get.unique.col.values(this.unit.data[,output.meta.data %>% colnames]))
    }
  
  #if there are non-zero rows for this unit, compute adjacencies
  if(nrow(this.unit.data) > 0) {

      #get rows associated with this unit
      unit.rows = this.unit.data$Rows
    
      #get times, or if window model (ie, not times given), use rows
      if(use.window) {
        this.time = Rows
      } else {
        this.time = this.context[,f.time]
      }
      
      #print(this.time)
      
      if(use.modes) these.modes = this.context[,f.mode]
    
      #loop on  unit (ie, response) rows
      for (response in unit.rows){
        #for each response, find earlier chats
        
        response.time = this.time[response]
        ground = which(this.time <= response.time)
    
        #if there is a limit on how far back in time to look, take only rows
        #that are after that limit
        if(!any(is.na(f.window.limit))) {
          ground = which(this.time[ground] >= (response.time - f.window.limit))
        }
        
        #find row numbers of the current response row WITHIN GROUND
        response.in.ground = which(ground == response)

        #get codes for ground and response
        response.codes = as.matrix(this.context[response, f.codes])
        ground.codes = as.matrix(this.context[ground, f.codes])
        

        #compute decays
        #
        #Get modes, if needed
        ground.modes = NA
        if(use.modes) ground.modes = these.modes[ground]

        #get decays -- get.decay.modes handles whether to use modes or not
        my.decays = get.decay.modes(
            now = response.time,
            event.time = this.time[ground],
            modes = ground.modes,
            decay.function = f.decay
        )

        #apply decays to ground
        
        #if there is only a single line of data, multiple by scalar
        if(length(my.decays) == 1) {
          ground.codes = ground.codes * my.decays 
        } else {
          
        #otherwise this is a bit of fancy math that multiplies each row of the matrix 
        #by a different scalar from a vector of scalars 
          ground.codes = t(t(ground.codes) %*% diag(my.decays))
        }
        
        #find the ground code corresponsing the the response line
        #since the response line is in its own "window" for connections
        #and we can't assume that for its mode the decay at time_0 = 1
        this.response.in.ground = t(ground.codes[response.in.ground,])

        #collapse the ground codes into a vector colsums
        this.ground = t(as.matrix(.colSums(ground.codes, m = length(ground), n = length(f.codes))))

        #compute connections
        this.connection.matrix = crossprod(this.ground, response.codes)
        
        #compute the connections from the response to itself
        this.self.connection = crossprod(this.response.in.ground, response.codes)

        #remove self-references in response code from from the adjacency counts
        diag(this.connection.matrix) = diag(this.connection.matrix) - diag(this.self.connection)
        
        #weighting function lets us account for inflation of connections
        #due to multiplication of weighted code values
        #we do the same thing in weighted ENA
        this.code.matrix = this.code.matrix + f.weighting.function(this.connection.matrix)
        
        #go back to next row for this unit
        
      } #done looping over rows for this unit
      
  } #end of if statement -- the above is all skipped if there are no
    #non-zero rows to loop over for the unit
  
  #for this unit...
 
  #apply mask to the adjacency matrix
  
  if(use.mask) this.code.matrix = this.code.matrix * mask

  #first, deal with directed matrix
  
  #add directed adjacency matrix to the context
  f.contexts[[this.hoo]]$directed.adjacency = this.code.matrix
  
  #construct directed adjacency vector
  directed.adjacency.vectors = rbind(directed.adjacency.vectors, as.vector(this.code.matrix))

  
  #next, undirected
  
  #commenting this out keeps self-connections in undirecteed matrix
  #but it will be removed for ena adjacency vectors
  #diag(this.code.matrix) = 0
  
  #turn directed into undirected
  
  #upper triangle is some of directed connections
  this.code.matrix[upper.tri(this.code.matrix)] =
    this.code.matrix[upper.tri(this.code.matrix)] + this.code.matrix[lower.tri(this.code.matrix)]
  #make matrix symmetrical
  this.code.matrix[lower.tri(this.code.matrix)] = NA
  
  #add undirected matrix to context 
  f.contexts[[this.hoo]]$undirected.adjacancy = this.code.matrix
  
  #create undirected vector
  undirected.adjacency.vectors = rbind(
    undirected.adjacency.vectors,
    this.code.matrix[upper.tri(this.code.matrix)]
    )
 
  #go back to next context

}#done looping over contexts

#construct output
output = list()

#add contexts (with additions of adjacency matrices) to output
output$contexts = f.contexts
#add additional information for modeling
output$directed.adjacency.vectors = directed.adjacency.vectors
output$units = f.units

#construct information for ENA set
# browser()
enadata = structure(list(), class = c("ENAdata", "list"))
enadata$adjacency.matrix = rENA:::namesToAdjacencyKey(f.codes)
enadata$codes = f.codes
enadata$model = "TMA"
enadata$raw = data.table::as.data.table(f.raw)
enadata$units = f.units
enadata$meta.data = data.table::as.data.table(output.meta.data)
enadata$metadata = data.table::as.data.table(output.meta.data)
enadata$adjacency.vectors = data.table::as.data.table(undirected.adjacency.vectors)
enadata$accumulated.adjacency.vectors = data.table::as.data.table(undirected.adjacency.vectors)

output$for.ena$enadata=enadata

#if ena set is requested, construct ena set using rENA:::ena.set
#and remove the information used to create it
if(return.ena.set) {
  output$ena.set = rENA:::ena.set(enadata) #output$for.ena)
  output$for.ena = NULL
}

return(output)

}


```


To test the model, I created two delay functions. One is the original decay function. One has a longer decay time.


```{r TMAaccumulation}

#this tests the main accumulation function for TMA

#original decay function
chat.decay.function = decay.function

#decay function with a longer decay time
view.decay.function = function(x) return(-0.0039*x^3 + 0.0661*x^2 - 0.3507*x + 1)


#construct list for passing to accumulate,units
modal.decay.function = list()
modal.decay.function$view = view.decay.function
modal.decay.function$chat = chat.decay.function

my.accumulation = accumulate.units(context.object = these.hoos, 
                                   codes = c('Data',
                                              'Technical.Constraints',
                                              'Performance.Parameters',
                                              'Client.and.Consultant.Requests',
                                              'Design.Reasoning',
                                              'Collaboration'
                                              ), 
                                   time.column = "time", 
                                   #decay.function = decay.function, 
                                   decay.function = modal.decay.function, 
                                   mode.column = "CommunicationType",
                                   weight.by = sqrt,
                                   time.limit = 7,
                                   meta.data = c("CONFIDENCE.Pre", "CONFIDENCE.Change"),
                                   return.ena.set = TRUE)

#show results
print("For ENA:")
my.accumulation$for.ena
print("Contexts (with adjacency matrices):")
my.accumulation$contexts
print("units:")
my.accumulation$units
print("Directed adjacency vectors")
my.accumulation$directed.adjacency.vectors
print("::")

#show delays for the two functions
print("original decay function from t=0 to t=9")
chat.decay.function( (1:10)-1 )
print("Slower decay function from t=0 to t=9")
view.decay.function( (1:10)-1 )
```
